01-progress.png.five_seconds: Our best public score fell from 265.8 to 223.3 s over 75 uploads; the off-block time seen in ADS-B ground tracks gave the largest step (−14.3 s), and each step of 2.5 s or more has a label that says what we did.
01-progress.png.does_it: yes: four labels of the form gain then what we did, each with a leader to the dot where its step ends; no step after upload 52 reaches 2.5 s, so the steps of uploads 64 to 73 have no label; first and best scores as plain text by their dots; no phase bands, dates or upload numbers in the labels; no line crosses a label

02-clock.png.five_seconds: Timing the first ADS-B point back to the stand puts the off-block clock 3 to 7 minutes earlier at the median, at every airport.
02-clock.png.does_it: yes: the sketch shows old and new clock; the dots read 2.8 to 7.1 min

03-coverage.png.five_seconds: The share of departures with an ADS-B clock moved sharply between 2025 and 2026: Rome July lost it, Heathrow July and Madrid January gained it.
03-coverage.png.does_it: yes: arrows mark the large moves; two colours with a key; small values sit below their dots

04-join-window.png.five_seconds: Every joined 2025 departure has its block time within ±3,606 s of the plan; outside the window, no plan joins.
04-join-window.png.does_it: yes: the histogram ends inside the red lines; the shaded sides say what a missing plan means

05-placeholders.png.five_seconds: At Rome, 8.4 % of delayed or early departures keep the scheduled time as block time; no other airport exceeds 1.5 %.
05-placeholders.png.does_it: yes: one red bar against grey bars, with the count

06-stand-bound.png.five_seconds: When another aircraft parks at the stand after 18 min, a taxi of 121.1 min has a floor of 103.1 min, far above the earlier model's 52.3 min.
06-stand-bound.png.does_it: yes: three bars on one time axis with the stand event marked

07-runway-sequence.png.five_seconds: The sequence network sees twelve departures of one runway in take-off order; its twin without neighbours enters the stack with a negative weight.
07-runway-sequence.png.does_it: yes: the bars show 4 before, 4 core, 4 after; the flow shows data, model, combination and output shapes with +0.48 and −0.21

08-early-stopping.png.five_seconds: Scoring the early stop only on served rows let the stacker train 4.4 and 7.2 times longer.
08-early-stopping.png.does_it: yes: two arrows from amber to teal dots with the round counts and the result line

09-alignment.png.five_seconds: Added up, the board kept about 0.8 of the local gain; single steps scatter on both sides of the 0.83 line.
09-alignment.png.does_it: yes: two panels with one-to-one and 0.83 lines; every point labelled with its upload

10-pipeline.png.five_seconds: Upload 73 runs top to bottom: five inputs, two feature steps, tree models with the September entry, a clock head and four other views (the GRU box with its dark-day twin), three combinations, four recording rules, the quarter step of upload 64, then one group with the three later steps (five steps outside the linear stack, half of a second-level LightGBM correction, a per-airport step toward the airport-traffic transformer), one output; the key gives each shape and colour its role.
10-pipeline.png.does_it: yes: Mermaid diagram, taller, arrows with room, key in two rows, text readable at 800 px wide; one arrow per feature box into the tree-model group keeps crossings few; the later steps sit in one labelled group, and the five-step box has hand line breaks
10-pipeline.png.source: src/10-pipeline.mmd, rendered on the Mac with @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli 12.0.0 and local Chrome (-s 2 -b white)
